newsitem.title: USA: Manufacturers group see 2.5 pct US 1997 GDP growth.
newsitem.headline: Manufacturers group see 2.5 pct US 1997 GDP growth.

text.p: National Association of Manufacturers predicted U.S. gross domestic product would grow by 2.5 percent in 1997.
Inflation should remain in check at just over two percent, the group said in its annual economic outlook released here on Thursday.

A gradual decline in the value of the dollar and stronger growth overseas next year will boost exports 6.2 percent, the group said. Investment in business equipment should jump 8.8 percent while residential construction is forecast to decline by 4.6 percent, the group said.

"The economy's current stability stems from a general flattening of the business cycle, thanks to lower inflation, better control of inventories and smarter monetary and fiscal policies," association president Jerry Jasinowski said.

The group did mention several risks that could push the economy off its stable path, however. Failure to enact a budget agreement in Washington could cause long-term interest rates to spike, reducing growth by about half a percentage point, the group said.
Also, high levels of personal debt remain a threat.
Strong employments and income gains along with increased wealth from the booming stock market should offset the high debt problem, the group said.
However, a major international shock, such as a rise in oil prices or a trade war, would weaken export growth.
The manufacturers group also endorsed proposals to revise the consumer price index made Wednesday by a bipartisan panel chaired by Michael Boskin.
"Congress and the administration should act promptly to implement the general thrust of the recommendations of the Boskin commission," the group said.
The Boskin commission urged a variety of changes, including legislation to alter the way tax brackets and costly programs like Social Security are adjusted for cost-of-living changes.
Such changes would help balance the federal budget and move the economy on a track of higher growth, the group said.
